items.summary_raw: ⚡️ 🔴 New German decisions regarding the German intelligence service: The German government has approved comprehensive reforms for the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), allowing agents to actively move to confront external threats, and not be limited to just collecting intelligence; according to a report by "BILD" newspaper. Under the proposed law, BND agents can carry out measures such as disabling weapons, replacing real bombs with safe (inert) models, deleting electronic data, and other subversive operations, to prevent attacks against Germany or allied countries. In cases of extreme emergency, war, and self-defense, agents are even allowed to use "kinetic means," including firearms. However, targeted assassinations and the formation of assassination squads will remain prohibited. Before these reforms, BND agents sometimes possessed accurate information about threats, but they were not legally authorized to intervene. For example, in some cases, the locations of Iranian missiles that were to be delivered to Hezbollah were identified, but agents did not have permission to disable them. items.title: Europe heatwave live: Temperatures of 40C expected in Spain, with amber heat health warning in place across large parts of UK
items.summary_raw:
In France, 80 departments have been placed on an orange heat warning

Over in England, the amber warning by the Met Office stretches from London to Sheffield, covering parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire and is in place from 9am to midnight on Thursday, PA reported.

Met Office forecaster Alex Burkill said:

“Temperatures [in areas covered by the amber warning] could reach highs of around 36, 37, possibly 38C.

Now when you get these sorts of high temperatures, well that’s when we could see impacts to our infrastructure, our railway lines, our roads, they are not designed for this sort of heat.

items.title: Millions face higher water bills as suppliers allowed £3.4bn extra spending
items.summary_raw:
Firms in England and Wales seek to fund measures including supporting new homes and datacentres

  • Business live – latest updates

Millions of households in England and Wales face higher bills after water companies were given the green light to spend £3.4bn more than planned, including to support new homes and datacentres.

The new spending will come on top of the £104bn programme of investment approved by the regulator that had already meant water bills will rise by 36% over the second half of the decade.

items.title: India fuels worldwide jump in planned coal production
items.summary_raw:
Rise in new mine proposals, mainly in states of Odisha and Jharkhand, comes despite plateau in global demand

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.

Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.

items.title: Israel seeking to 'remove Palestine from world's agenda', Erdogan says
items.summary_raw:
Israel seeking to 'remove Palestine from world's agenda', Erdogan says

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday accused Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's government of seeking to "remove Palestine" from the world's agenda. 

"The aim of the Netanyahu government is to remove Palestine from the common agenda of humanity by profiting from chaos and new conflicts in the region," Erdogan said at a joint news conference with his Palestinian counterpart Mahmoud Abbas in Ankara. 

"No matter what they do, they will not succeed. The Palestinian cause will continue to grow in people's hearts as they try to destroy it," he said, vowing Turkey would fight for the establishment of a Palestinian state.

items.title: Erdogan eyes expansion of regional defence pact
items.summary_raw:
Erdogan eyes expansion of regional defence pact

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said he hoped more countries would join a defence agreement signed last week between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed on Friday.

"Our vision for it is not limited to the three countries," the Turkish leader told Asharq Al-Awsat. "Rather we aspire for it to grow, and perhaps appropriate conditions will emerge one day for all countries of the region to gather under its umbrella." 

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Saturday said Turkey expected Egypt to join the pact "in the next stage", telling the Anadolu state news agency only "a few technical issues" stood in the way. 

Egypt has not commented on the agreement nor on the remarks by Fidan, who will visit Cairo on Thu

items.title: Heat, algae and AI: proposed datacenter could damage Everglades, experts warn
items.summary_raw:
Plans for hyperscale datacenter in Palm Beach county prompt concerns over water and electricity demands

About 16 miles (26km) south-west of Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Largo estate, near the northern edge of the Florida Everglades, developers have proposed a hyperscale datacenter on a 202-acre (82-hectare) parcel of land surrounded by water. Local environmentalists warn that the proposed 600MW datacenter in western Palm Beach county could damage the wetlands, which the federal government and the state of Florida have spent a combined $6bn to restore after decades of drainage and development.

One concern is that the datacenter could exacerbate an existing issue of toxic bacterial blooms in a water system which has already been stressed by drought, fertilizer runoff and warm water temperatures. In recent summers, the bright blooms of blue-green algae have covered nearly half of Lake Okeechobee, which feeds into the Everglades.

The company added that repeated targeting have lead to severe damage to the Zawiya power station, and has forced it to withdraw its technical teams.

It warned that the attacks may cause more delays in maintenance and restoration of electricity services.

The Romanian Naval Component Command contacted Ukraine, which confirmed that the aircraft did not belong to Ukrainian forces.

items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender Iran is adapting its tactics to wear down U.S. air defenses, and exploit dwindling interceptor stocks, according to new reporting from The New York Times.  During five days of attacks on U.S. bases in Jordan last month, Iran combined drones with maneuvering ballistic missiles to overwhelm defensive systems. On July 17, one missile penetrated the defenses at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, killing 3 U.S. soldiers and wounding more than 100.  The scale of the expenditure is becoming increasingly important: the U.S. has fired more than 1,500 Patriot interceptors during the war and reportedly has fewer than 1,700 remaining, while producing only about 600 Patriots in all of 2025. On one day during the Jordan attacks, U.S. forces reportedly fired around 50 Patriots, at roughly $4 million each.  Iran has also demonstrated other adaptations, including using drones to provide targeting data that helped shoot down a U.S. F-15E in April and expanding attacks through partners such as the Houthis to force U.S. forces to defend against threats from multiple directions.  The Pentagon continues to publicly deny that the U.S. has a munitions shortage. tweet

items.title: The Guardian view on wildfires: firefighters can’t handle this crisis alone | Editorial
items.summary_raw:
The response to this summer’s record heat and drought should be led by ministers – not left to the emergency services

The wildfire that began on protected heathland in the New Forest in Hampshire on Sunday was reported to be under control on Tuesday. But with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or higher in parts of England on Thursday, the risk of further outbreaks remains high. Firefighters responded to 185 wildfires in the first 10 days of August. In coastal Suffolk, conservationists and locals are counting the cost of the blaze that devastated Dunwich Heath. Its vegetation and rare bird populations are expected to take decades to recover.

Although the immediate cause of many wildfires is litter, the risks are elevated by heat and drought, and repeated warnings from climate scientists do not necessarily lessen the shock and distress caused. items.title: Inside the growing rift between Iran’s dealmakers and ultraconservatives
items.summary_raw:
Inside the growing rift between Iran’s dealmakers and ultraconservatives

Iran’s political landscape appears to have entered a new phase as two competing camps emerge: those advocating a deal with the United States and those determined to block any agreement.

Principlists have intensified their pressure on reformist President Masoud Pezeshkian and conservative Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, both of whom are seeking to reach an agreement with Washington and bring an end to almost six months of hostilities.

Principlists fear that any deal could marginalise them politically and weaken their influence over Iran’s future direction.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), the international reference point for maritime security incidents, has received a report of an attack on a cargo ship in Bab al-Mandab off the coast of Mocha from an "unknown projectile" which resulted "in casualties".

Yemeni official sources from the coast guard and military say at least three crew members have been killed. They say the attack came from the Houthis, which control much of Yemen's Red Sea coast.

Until now, Yemen's Houthis had only targeted tankers carrying Saudi oil in the Bab al-Mandab, not container ships.

items.summary_raw:
Met Office says this warning will likely cause ‘adverse’ health effects with travel and power generation also possibly affected

The Guardian’s environment editor, Fiona Harvey, has written a useful explainer about the UK public services that are struggling in the extreme weather. You can read it in full here:

There’s only one solution in the end to the drought now declared across most of England and that’s rain, says Hannah Cloke, professor of hydrology at the University of Reading.

An important consequence of drought is that very dry soils can become less able to absorb rainfall when it does arrive. This can increase surface runoff and can even contribute to localised flash flooding, particularly if rain falls intensely over a short period.

The current situation highlights the need to improve long-term resilience to both drought and flood risk as climate variability increases, and shows one more damaging impact of the burning of fossil fuels.

Iran will bring back 95 million cubic metres of gas to its production cycle by the end of September, oil minister Mohsen Paknejad said on Tuesday, according to the oil ministry's news outlet, as Tehran conducts repairs on energy infrastructure targeted by Israel and the US.

In July, a senior government official said Iran expects to restore around 100 million cubic metres per day of natural gas production capacity "within the coming months", after air strikes removed about 230 million cubic metres from output since the war started on 28 February.

items.title: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test
items.summary_raw:
In today’s newsletter: As we enter our fifth summer heatwave, Andy Burnham’s government is looking at what the UK should do with its remaining North Sea oil and gas

Good morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.”

This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh, now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new government: to drill or not to drill, baby?

Two sites are the focus of fierce debate. Yesterday, a public consultation on whether to greenlight extraction at one of them – Jackdaw – closed. Next Monday, it’ll be the same for the other, Rosebank. Andy Burnham

The head of the military intelligence department for Libya's eastern-based forces led by Khalifa Haftar was killed in a targeted assassination on Monday, Anadolu Agency reported citing a Libyan security official.

An explosive device planted under Fawzi al-Mansouri's vehicle exploded in al-Sayyida Aisha residential neighborhood in eastern Benghazi.

According to the report, the official described the incident as a "terrorist attack," however, no official statement has been issued so far on the assassination.

Based on the latest Fire Service update, the situation regarding the wildfire that started in Kouvaras on Monday morning was considerably improved, with strong firefighting forces now only dealing with numerous still-smoking spots within its perimeter. Earlier, the advancing flames had ruined installations at a poultry-farming unit near the village of Agios Stylianos.

items.title: July was hottest month ever recorded in US as heatwaves scorched country
items.summary_raw:
Scientists have made clear that the elevated heat in the US was being amplified by the human-caused climate crisis

July was the hottest month ever recorded in the US, with repeated, scorching heatwaves across much of the country helping shatter all previous monthly temperature records stretching back over the full 132 years of reliable measurements.

Last month’s average temperature was 3.3F (1.8C) higher than the 20th century average for the contiguous United States, which excludes Alaska and Hawaii, according to new data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).

items.summary_raw: Visioner 🚨🇺🇸🇺🇦 BREAKING | President Donald Trump has reversed a decision that would have allowed Ukraine to obtain production licenses for Patriot air-defense technology, according to The Telegraph.  The decision was reportedly driven by concerns in Washington that some of the system's most sensitive U.S. technologies could eventually fall into Russian hands.  One of the central concerns involves the Ka-band homing radar used by the PAC-3 interceptor, manufactured by Boeing. The technology is considered so advanced and highly classified that the White House reportedly restricts its export even to some of America's closest allies.  The reversal represents a significant setback for Kyiv's efforts to establish greater domestic production capacity for Patriot-related systems and reduce its dependence on limited deliveries of U.S.-made interceptors.  For Ukraine, the challenge now becomes finding a production model that can expand its Patriot capabilities while satisfying Washington's strict technology-security requirements. Great Britain’s biggest household energy supplier is calling on its customers to use less electricity this week during the deepest solar eclipse in almost 30 years.

items.title: UAE oil company announces new investments to bypass Hormuz
items.summary_raw:
UAE oil company announces new investments to bypass Hormuz

Abu Dhabi National Oil Co (Adnoc), the Emirate's national oil company, announced plans to construct a new gas export facility to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

The company reported its income for the second quarter of 2026 earlier today, beating forecasts with a net income of $665m and strong guidance for the rest of the year, contingent on exports being fully restored in the fourth quarter.

Adnoc also announced its intention to construct a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facility on the eastern coast of the UAE, which would allow it to move LNG out of the Persian Gulf without having to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

The company's ships have come under repeated attacks while transiting through Hormuz, with three of its vessels having been attacked

items.title: Western Europe Sets New Temperature Record as Heat Waves, Drought and Wildfires Pummel the Region
items.summary_raw: PARIS (AP) — Europe is enduring another exceptionally hot summer, with persistent heat waves fueling wildfires, prolonged drought and new temperature records across the continent, while Western Europe has set a new average temperature record for the June-July period. The average temperature in Western Europe for June and July reached 21.62 C (70.92 F), according to the European climate agency Copernicus, surpassing the previous record set in 2022. The extreme heat has affected countries across Europe since May, with France, in particular, facing repeated heat waves and record-breaking temperatures. The latest episode is expected to bring temperatures approaching 40 C (104 F) in southeastern France from Tuesday onward, as the country braces for its fifth heat wave alert of the season. “Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over western Europe, the extreme temperatures also amplified widespread drought. items.summary_raw: Situation on the Stepnohirsk & Orikhiv directions, Zaporizhzhia Oblast:  Over the last two weeks, both Russian and Ukrainian forces have continued their assault operations, with Russian forces launching a new series of attacks aimed at recapturing previously lost positions.  In the west, Ukrainian forces cleared the southern dachas of Prymorske from earlier Russian infiltrations and expanded their foothold south of the Sukhyy River in northern Plavni. From there, they pushed further south, improving their positions in the central part of Plavni, where Russia is now dropping KAB glide-bombs. Other assault groups advanced further down the highway and are attempting to reach the northern outskirts of Kamyanske.  To the northeast, the Ukrainians finally cleared the remaining part of Stepnohirsk north of the Sukhyy River after multiple months of intense fighting, before subsequently establishing control over Aharna Street south of the river. From here, they are attempting to enter the southernmost high-rise micro-district of the town. items.title: Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai
items.summary_raw:
Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland

More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.

Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas.

items.title: As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes? | John Harris
items.summary_raw:
Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities

Amid headlines about the UK’s drought, Europe’s wildfires and impossible global temperatures, it was 28C when I arrived in Slough last Monday. I was there to look around Slough Trading Estate, a place that might once have conjured up images of the TV comedy The Office, many of whose laughs came at the expense of this overgrown patch of suburbia, 20-odd miles west of London.

But these days, this area of town – an incongruous mixture of old-school businesses such as Mr Clutch and Angling Direct, and vast, metal-clad leviathans that look like something pulled from JG Ballard – has become a byword for the constant expansion of datacentres, those hulking symbols of the vast computing power that big tech now requires, not least because of the ever-more complex workings of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Cyprus Natural Gas To Supply Europe by First Half of 2028, Minister Says, As EU Seeks New Sources
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA, Cyprus (AP) — European consumers can expect natural gas from an undersea deposit off Cyprus to help meet their energy needs as early as March 2028, the island nation's energy minister said. Michael Damianos said the East Mediterranean is fast becoming an alternative energy source for European nations as Russia’s war in Ukraine and upheaval in the Middle East compel the continent to seek out new sources. Damianos said partners TotalEnergies of France and Italy's Eni made a final decision last month to proceed with developing the Cronos natural gas field off Cyprus’ southern coast. The project will be the first time gas from east Mediterranean deposits is supplied to European markets. “It’s important for Europe at this time because of the war in Ukraine, because of this situation in the Middle East, that Cyprus is going to be an alternative source of gas,” Damianos told The Associated Press in an exclusive interview Friday.

Saudi Arabia has condemned the attack on an oil tanker operated by the UAE’s ADNOC while transiting the Strait of Hormuz as “an assault on global energy security”.

The UAE had blamed Iran for the attack, condemned also by Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar and Syria.

In a statement, the Saudi ministry of foreign affairs said: “These reprehensible attacks constitute an assault on the security and safety of maritime navigation, as well as on the security of global energy supplies.”

The statement added that the kingdom “holds Iran responsible for the consequences of its continued acts of aggression and calls on Iran to immediately cease these violations”.

items.title: OSINTdefender The Pentagon is now giving defense contractors 21 days to come up with ways to dramatically accelerate weapons production as the Iran war continues to eat through U.S…
items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender The Pentagon is now giving defense contractors 21 days to come up with ways to dramatically accelerate weapons production as the Iran war continues to eat through U.S. stockpiles.  Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg directed industry to propose faster delivery schedules, increased production and investments in new manufacturing capacity.  The scale of the depletion is significant. The Pentagon says the U.S. has expended more than 850 Tomahawks, 1,000 Patriot/THAAD interceptors and 1,300 tactical ballistic missiles in the early stages of the war.  A CSIS estimate cited by the Washington Post puts global Patriot inventories at under 827, down from roughly 2,200 before the war, while THAAD inventories have fallen from 452 to fewer than 278.  The Pentagon has announced framework agreements to expand production, including the recent effort to triple PAC-3 production and quadruple production of key THAAD components. But these agreements still require congressional funding. tweet

items.summary_raw: The Pentagon is pressing U.S. defense companies to rapidly boost weapons production after the Iran war sharply depleted missile stocks.  Firms have 21 days to propose faster deliveries, expanded factories, and increased capacity.  The biggest concern is air-defense ammunition: Patriot inventories reportedly fell from about 2,200 to under 827, while THAAD stocks dropped from 452 to under 278.   The Pentagon is pursuing major production deals, including a $58.6 billion Lockheed Martin agreement, but much of the expansion depends on a $1.15 trillion defense spending bill stalled in Congress.  Source: WaPo

items.title: ‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn
items.summary_raw:
Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027

El Niño, a recurring climate phenomenon marked by above-average sea surface temperatures, when changes in wind patterns allow warmer water to spread across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, could spell a wet winter for portions of the western and south-eastern US, climate models show. Coastal areas may be at elevated risk of flooding, experts warn.

Climate scientists predict this year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperatures climb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century. The weather system is expected to intensify in the fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).

items.title: Turkey says Saudi-Pakistan defence pact mirrors NATO’s Article 5, Egypt could also join
items.summary_raw:
Turkey says Saudi-Pakistan defence pact mirrors NATO’s Article 5, Egypt could also join

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan says the new defence agreement between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia is technically equivalent to NATO’s Article 5 mutual defence clause and does not target Iran.

Fidan told Turkey’s Anadolu news agency that the three countries would establish a ministerial committee resembling NATO’s decision-making structure. The pact will also have a general secretariat based in Saudi Arabia.

Egypt could join the alliance once the parties resolve outstanding technical issues, Fidan added.

Vance said the US would continue working to “maximize the amount of oil” passing through the strait to keep fuel and energy prices low for Americans.

items.title: 'Foreign forces must leave': Iran says regional countries can ensure their own security
items.summary_raw:
'Foreign forces must leave': Iran says regional countries can ensure their own security

Ali Akbar Velayati, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, has called for foreign forces to leave the region, saying their presence is the “main factor of insecurity”.

items.title: Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up
items.summary_raw:
Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions

Record-low water levels in the Danube have exposed remnants of Europe’s Nazi past, with dozens of second world war ships emerging from the riverbed during an intense drought.

In the middle of the river on the Serbian and Romanian border, a broken-up hull was visible on a sandbank that is normally underwater. Other vessels were partly submerged, some still believed to be laden with weapons.

The Al Areesh departed Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG terminal and transited the Strait of Hormuz outbound on July 29, utilizing Iran's traffic separation scheme, according to publicly available AIS tracking data from http://MarineTraffic.com.  Its continued inability to proceed beyond the apparent blockade line is notable because the vessel does not appear to have loaded cargo in Iran or be associated with an Iranian port, and therefore does not appear to fit the publicly understood criteria for vessels subject to the U.S. naval blockade. items.summary_raw: BREAKING: The US Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act by a vote of 86-11.  The bill now heads to the House, which returns after the August recess.  The core provision authorizes the President to impose targeted tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas.  The bill also extends Iran sanctions, keeping restrictions on Iran's energy and arms sectors from expiring by renewing the 1996 Iran Sanctions Act through 2031. The agreement stops short of detailing automatic military obligations, but it formalizes closer defense coordination between three of the Muslim world's most influential militaries. Saudi Arabia has come under repeated Iranian attacks since the start of Operation Epic Fury, Turkey fields NATO's second-largest military, and Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority nation.  The pact follows nearly a year of negotiations and reflects growing concern that regional states may need to rely more on their own security architecture as the Iran conflict continues to threaten Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping. Turkish and Saudi officials stressed the agreement is defensive in nature and is not directed at any specific country. tweet

items.summary_raw: Visioner 🚨🇮🇷🛢️⚠️ Iran's oil exports are reportedly grinding to a halt as the U.S. naval blockade tightens. New shipping data suggests Tehran's most important export terminal has been virtually idle for a week, threatening one of the regime's main sources of revenue.  According to the Financial Times, no oil tanker has loaded crude at Iran's Kharg Island terminal for at least a week, indicating that the renewed U.S. naval blockade may have effectively halted Iran's crude exports.  The Kharg terminal, which handles around 90% of Iran's oil exports, has been largely inactive since July 31. Satellite imagery reportedly shows all three loading berths empty, while only 16 vessels remain in the anchorage area, the lowest number recorded since early last month.  The monitoring group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI) says no tanker carrying Iranian crude has successfully departed the Persian Gulf since July 12.  For now, Tehran continues to receive revenue from cargoes shipped during the ceasefire period, but the Financial Times reports that this income is expected to dry up in the coming weeks if exports do not resume. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told reporters on Wednesday that Hamas has "fulfilled many of the responsibilities" to implement the US-backed Gaza peace plan while Israel continues to undermine the process.

Fidan warned that Israel is using negotiations to advance its own policies rather than achieve a settlement, adding that Israel’s expansionist policies could lead to a global crisis. 

"Israel has no intention or plan for peace," he said.

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

The population of Firminy, south-east France, has been dwindling for decades. Its recent history is one of factory closures in a region built by steel, and locals tell me that many people leave for better opportunities in neighbouring Saint-Étienne, or to live in the Haute-Loire’s countryside.

On the top of a hill, however, stands Firminy’s pride: l’Unité d’Habitation, an imposing tower of concrete designed by Le Corbusier. The architect’s final project is an oddity – a building for people, where two-thirds of the apartments are dedicated to habitations à loyer modéré (or HLM – social housing); but also a piece of history, whose facade and roof were listed as monuments historiques in 1993.

items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender The estimated cost of President Trump's proposed Trump class battleship has climbed sharply, with the Congressional Budget Office now projecting 15 nuclear-powered guided missile battleships would cost roughly $275 billion, about 50% higher than earlier Navy estimates.  CBO estimates the lead ship could cost $23.4 billion and take eight years or more to build, while follow on ships are projected at just over $18 billion each. For comparison, that would make the lead Trump-class battleship more expensive than even a Ford class nuclear powered aircraft carrier, currently the most expensive warship in the U.S. Navy, with future Ford-class carriers estimated to cost around $14 billion each.  The higher costs are driven in part by the decision to switch the design to nuclear propulsion, while critics also point to the Navy's recent struggles delivering new ship classes on time and on budget. tweet
